events.text: Objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available in mid-1962 to justify Deere & Company investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, leveraging its tractor engineering.. Constraints: Limited to public sources published before mid-1962; no internal company data.; Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.; Evidence must address demand, willingness to pay, and feasibility of reaching individual buyers.; Must consider existing dealer network and any existing consumer products.. Alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., small‑holder farming, home gardening, or a niche industrial application).; 2) Expand the existing dealer network to reach individual buyers directly without a differentiated proposition.; 3) No expansion: continue focusing on current B2B markets and existing product lines.; 4) License tractor technology to third‑party manufacturers for consumer applications..

T1: Homeowners will adopt lawn tractors because they reduce labor cost and increase lawn care efficiency compared to manual tools. Who benefits: Homeowners seeking higher lawn quality and lower labor expenses.. Why behaviour changes: If a lawn tractor demonstrably saves time and money compared to hand mowing, homeowners will purchase it to achieve a better lawn and free up time for other activities.. How value is captured: Deere can capture value by selling tractors at a premium price and through dealer margins, leveraging its existing dealer network to reach individual buyers.. Assumptions: Homeowners have sufficient disposable income to afford a lawn tractor in 1962.; They are aware of the time savings and cost benefits.; Dealer network can effectively communicate these benefits to consumers.. Predictions: Surveyed homeowners will indicate willingness to pay a price premium for a lawn tractor that saves at least 30 minutes per lawn.; Dealer sales data will show an increase in sales when a lawn tractor is introduced compared to a period without it..

T2: Homeowners will adopt lawn tractors because they signal status and community acceptance, and owning one becomes a social norm that drives purchase. Who benefits: Homeowners seeking social recognition and belonging within their neighborhood.. Why behaviour changes: If lawn tractors become visible status symbols and neighbors who own them are perceived as successful, homeowners will purchase to fit in and signal their own success.. How value is captured: Deere can capture value by positioning the tractor as a lifestyle accessory, commanding premium pricing, and leveraging dealer networks to create community-driven demand.. Assumptions: Neighborhood peer pressure influences purchase decisions in 1962.; Homeowners associate lawn tractors with social status and community acceptance.; Dealers can create a sense of community around the product.. Predictions: Surveyed homeowners will report that owning a lawn tractor is important for fitting in with neighbors.; Sales will be higher in neighborhoods where early adopters already own tractors..

Test "Survey of Homeowners on Lawn Tractor Purchase Motivation" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Participants view a product description of a 1962 lawn tractor (specifications, price, time savings claim). They are asked: "Which of the following best describes why you would buy this lawn tractor?" (a) Labor cost savings and time efficiency; (b) Status and community acceptance; (c) Other (specify). They also rate willingness to pay on a 1‑10 scale. The survey is targeted to homeowners in the United States who own a lawn (. Sample: 500 homeowners recruited via an online panel, balanced across age, income, and region.. Measure: Primary outcome: proportion of respondents selecting (a) labor cost savings/time efficiency as their primary reason. Secondary outcomes: average willingness to pay and stated importance of status/community acceptance.. Predictions: T1: At least 60% of respondents will select (a) as their primary reason, and willingness to pay will be positively correlated with the time savings claim.; T2: At least 60% of respondents will select (b) as their primary reason, and willingness to pay will be positively correlated with perceived status and community acceptance messaging.. Decision rule: If the proportion selecting (a) is ≥ 60% and willingness to pay is positively correlated with time savings claim (correlation ≥ 0.4), proceed with developing a differentiated consumer proposition focused on labor cost savings. If the proportion selecting (b) is ≥ 60% and willingness to pay is positively correlated with status/community messaging (correlation ≥ 0.4), proceed with developing a differentiated consumer proposition focused on status and community acceptance. If neither condition is met, . Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not commit to a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Instead, conduct the proposed survey test (X1) to empirically measure homeowner purchase motivation before investing further. The test will determine whether labor cost savings/time efficiency (T1) or status/community acceptance (T2) drives demand, allowing a data‑driven decision on which proposition to develop. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Do not commit to a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed survey test (X1) to empirically measure homeowner purchase motivation before investing further. The test will determine whether labor cost savings/time efficiency (T1) or status/community acceptance (T2) drives demand, allowing a data‑driven decision on which proposition to develop. Target customer: Homeowners in the United States who own a lawn and are considering a lawn tractor purchase.. Value proposition: A differentiated consumer proposition that either emphasizes labor cost savings and time efficiency or status and community acceptance, depending on which motivation is validated by the survey.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the survey test (X1) with 500 homeowners, measure the proportion selecting labor cost savings/time efficiency as primary reason and willingness to pay, and apply the decision rule to decide whether to develop a proposition focused on T1. Uncertainty: Both T1 and T2 remain uncertain due to lack of direct evidence from 1962 sources. The survey test is needed to resolve this uncertainty.. Would change if: If the survey shows at least 60% of respondents select labor cost savings/time efficiency as primary reason and willingness to pay is positively correlated with time savings claim (correlation ≥ 0.4).; If the survey shows at least 60% of respondents select status/community acceptance as primary reason and willingness to pay is positively correlated with perceived status messaging (correlation ≥ 0.4).. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

T1: Outdoor recreation enthusiasts will adopt 406 MHz distress beacons because they provide a reliable emergency backup in remote areas where other communication methods fail. Who benefits: Hikers, climbers, and other outdoor users who need a safety device that can be used in life-threatening situations.. Why behaviour changes: These users currently rely on mobile phones, radio, or satellite phones, but these can be damaged, lost, or out of range. A distress beacon offers a redundant, automatic alert that can be activated without user intervention.. How value is captured: ACR can sell the beacons directly to consumers through outdoor retailers or online, capturing the full retail price. The company also benefits from recurring revenue through rental or maintenance contracts.. Assumptions: Outdoor recreation participation rates in the U.S. remain stable or grow in 2002.; Consumers are willing to pay a premium for safety devices that work in remote environments.; Distribution channels (retailers, online) can reach this demographic.. Predictions: Surveyed outdoor recreation participants will indicate a willingness to purchase a 406 MHz distress beacon at a price point of $300-500.; Sales of the beacon will be concentrated in regions with high outdoor activity (e.g., national parks, mountain ranges)..

T2: Emergency preparedness organizations and government agencies will adopt 406 MHz distress beacons because they provide a standardized, interoperable solution for remote search and rescue, reducing response time and cost. Who benefits: Search and rescue (SAR) agencies, emergency management offices, and government departments responsible for public safety.. Why behaviour changes: Current SAR systems rely on multiple radio frequencies and protocols, leading to interoperability issues. A standardized 406 MHz distress beacon can be tracked by existing satellite networks, providing a single-source alert that can be used. How value is captured: ACR can sell the beacons to governments and NGOs at bulk rates, securing long-term contracts and recurring revenue from maintenance and upgrades. The company also benefits from brand association with reliable emergency. Assumptions: Government procurement cycles for emergency equipment are active in 2002.; Interoperability is a critical requirement for SAR agencies.; Price sensitivity is lower for public sector buyers compared to consumer markets.. Predictions: Government procurement requests for 406 MHz distress beacons will increase in 2002.; Sales will be concentrated in regions with high SAR demand (e.g., mountain ranges, remote coastal areas)..

Test "Consumer vs Government Purchase Intent Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: (A) Outdoor recreation users (hikers, climbers) and (B) Emergency preparedness organizations (SAR agencies, NGOs). Each participant views a product description of the 406 MHz distress beacon, highlighting its reliability in remote environments and interoperability (for T1) or its standardized, interoperable distress capability (for T2). They are then asked: "Would you purchase this beacon at a price of $300-500?" (binary yes/no).. Sample: 200 participants: 100 from outdoor recreation forums/clubs (representing T1) and 100 from emergency preparedness forums/NGOs (representing T2). Recruit via targeted ads to ensure geographic diversity.. Measure: Purchase intent (yes/no) for each participant group.. Predictions: T1: Outdoor recreation participants will show purchase intent at a rate of at least 40% (i.e., 40 out of 100 will say yes).; T2: Emergency preparedness participants will show purchase intent at a rate of at least 40% (i.e., 40 out of 100 will say yes).. Decision rule: If both groups achieve purchase intent rates ≥40%, both theories are considered supported. If only one group achieves the threshold, that theory is considered more likely. If neither group achieves the threshold, both theories are considered unlikely.. Cost: 18000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not commit to a new consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed test (Consumer vs Government Purchase Intent Test) to gather real purchase intent data before any investment. The test will clarify whether outdoor recreation users are willing to adopt the beacon at the proposed price point, which is essential for justifying a differentiated consumer product line. Until then, maintain the current product‑ Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns a label printer and packing errors, which does not address consumer demand, willingness to pay, or adoption behavior for the 406 MHz distress beacon. Therefore it neither supports nor contradicts T1. New claim: none. Evidence: SYN-D.

Recommendation: Do not commit to a new consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed Consumer vs Government Purchase Intent Test (200 participants, €18,000, 10 weeks) to gather real purchase intent data before any investment. The test will clarify whether outdoor recreation users are willing to adopt the beacon at the proposed price point, which is essential for justifying a differentiated consumer product line. Would change if: If the test shows purchase intent rates ≥40% for outdoor recreation participants, T1 would become likely and the recommendation would shift toward developing a consumer product.; If the test shows purchase intent rates ≥40% for emergency preparedness participants, T2 would become likely and the recommendation would shift toward pursuing a government/SAR market.. T1: Consumers with specific hearing needs (e.g., musicians, industrial workers) will purchase differentiated hearing protection if it offers performance or safety advantages beyond standard models. Who benefits: Consumers seeking specialized protection for their activities.. Why behaviour changes: They will switch to a differentiated product because they need performance that standard models cannot provide (e.g., sound fidelity for musicians, high-decibel protection for workers).. How value is captured: Hellberg can charge a premium for specialized features, sell through specialty channels, and build brand equity as a specialist.. Assumptions: Consumers identify their specific needs and are willing to pay a premium for tailored solutions.; There is measurable demand for specialized hearing protection in target segments.; Hellberg can develop and market specialized features that meet these needs.. Sample: 500 adults aged 18‑45, recruited via an online panel, balanced for gender and interest in music/fashion. Targeting musicians (n=200) and non‑musicians (n=300).. Measure: Average purchase intent score for the specialized model vs the fashion model, and average willingness to pay premium.. If neither condition is met, maintain current product focus (no expansion).. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Test "Musician vs Industrial Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase choice. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two conditions: (A) musician messaging emphasizing sound quality and musical performance; (B) industrial messaging emphasizing compliance and workplace fines. Both conditions receive the same product description (Hellberg earplugs) and price (€34.95). Participants indicate whether they would purchase the earplugs and the maximum price they would pay. The test also collects demographic data (age, occupation, music/. Sample: 200 participants: 100 early-career musicians (18-35, active in bands/orchestras) and 100 industrial workers (18-65, in noisy environments). Recruit via music forums, industry safety groups, and general panels to ensure geographic diversity.. Measure: Primary outcome: purchase intent (binary: "Would buy" vs "Would not buy"). Secondary: maximum price willing to pay (EUR).. Predictions: T1: Musician condition will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than Industrial condition.; T2: Industrial condition will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than Musician condition.. Decision rule: If the difference in purchase intent between the two conditions exceeds 10 percentage points (e.g., Musician condition at 65% vs Industrial at 55%), proceed to develop the differentiated proposition for the higher-intent segment. If the difference is ≤10. Cost: 12000 euros, 6 weeks.

Favours T1: Run the proposed Musician vs Industrial Messaging Test (200 participants, €12,000, 6 weeks) to empirically compare purchase intent and willingness to pay under musician-focused versus industrial-focused messaging. If the test shows a ≥10 percentage-point difference in purchase intent in favor of the musician condition, develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting musicians; otherwise, maintain current B2B‑ Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

The device, when it is a body composition analyzer which is not intended to diagnose or treat any medical condition, is exempt from the premarket notification procedures in subpart E of part 807 of this chapter

Based on medical evidence linking excess body fat to heart disease, diabetes and certain cancers, Tanita introduced the world’s first integrated body composition analyzer/scale to the professional markets in 1992.
Tanita is a world leader in precision electronic scales. With almost 50% of its domestic market share, the name Tanita is a household name in Japan.
In Japan, every household has a bathroom scale (health meter), and most nowadays keep track of your body composition.

T1: Health-conscious consumers will purchase a stand-on body-fat analyser for home use because they view it as a medical necessity for tracking body composition and preventing health risks. Who benefits: Consumers seeking to monitor health and reduce risk of chronic diseases.. Why behaviour changes: Growing public awareness of body composition's link to heart disease, diabetes, and cancers, combined with media coverage of bathroom scales as health tools, creates a perceived need for precise measurement.. How value is captured: Tanita can charge premium prices for a medical-grade device, sell through retail channels, and potentially bundle with health coaching services, capturing value through direct-to-consumer sales.. Assumptions: Consumers trust medical-grade body-fat measurement for health decisions.; Retail distribution channels exist for consumer products in 1993 Japan.; Price sensitivity is moderate for health-related devices.. Predictions: If offered at a price comparable to professional models, consumer purchase intent will be higher than for a generic home scale.; Sales will be concentrated in regions with higher obesity rates and stronger health awareness.; Repeat purchases for family members will occur within 12 months..

T2: Fitness enthusiasts will purchase a stand-on body-fat analyser because they view it as a performance tool for tracking progress and comparing results, creating a market driven by competition and self-improvement. Who benefits: Fitness-oriented consumers and health clubs seeking to provide advanced measurement tools.. Why behaviour changes: Growth of fitness culture in Japan, media coverage of body composition as a performance metric, and the desire to benchmark against peers drive demand for precise, measurable data.. How value is captured: Tanita can sell through fitness retailers and health clubs at premium prices, bundle with training programs, and offer data interpretation services, capturing value through recurring revenue and brand association with performance.. Assumptions: Fitness consumers prioritize measurable, actionable data for training.; Retail channels in 1993 stock fitness-related health devices.; Price sensitivity for performance-oriented consumers is lower than for general health devices.. Predictions: If marketed as a fitness tool, purchase intent will be higher than for a generic health device.; Sales will be concentrated in regions with higher participation in fitness activities.; Consumers will purchase multiple units for family or group use within 12 months..

Test "Consumer Purchase Intent Survey for Home Body-Fat Analyzer" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two conditions: Condition A sees a product description emphasizing medical necessity and health tracking; Condition B sees a product description emphasizing fitness performance and tracking progress. Both conditions receive the same price point (e.g., €250). After reading the description, participants indicate whether they would purchase the device and the number of units they would buy for family/friends within 12 months. The survey also asks about current ownership of a bathroom scale and self-reported BMI.. Sample: 500 Japanese adults aged 25-55, recruited via an online panel, balanced for gender and urban/rural residence.. Measure: Purchase intent (binary: would buy) and purchase quantity (units) for family/friends within 12 months.. Predictions: T1: Condition A will show higher purchase intent and quantity than Condition B because health-conscious consumers are motivated by medical necessity.; T2: Condition B will show higher purchase intent and quantity than Condition A because fitness-oriented consumers are motivated by performance tracking.. Decision rule: If Condition A’s purchase intent ≥ 40% and Condition B’s purchase intent ≤ 30%, conclude T1 is better supported. If Condition B’s purchase intent ≥ 40% and Condition A’s purchase intent ≤ 30%, conclude T2 is better supported. If both conditions show ≥ 40% intent, the evidence is inconclusive and we recommend no expansion.. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not launch a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed survey test to measure purchase intent under health-necessity versus fitness-performance framing before committing to any expansion. The test will clarify whether demand exists for a home body-fat analyzer and which value proposition would be most attractive. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns a label printer and packing errors, which does not address consumer purchase intent for a home body-fat analyzer. Recommendation: Do not launch a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed survey test to measure purchase intent under health-necessity versus fitness-performance framing before committing to any expansion. The test will clarify whether demand exists for a home body-fat analyzer and which value proposition would be most attractive. Target customer: Health-conscious consumers seeking medical necessity tracking (as indicated by public health awareness and media coverage of bathroom scales as health tools).. Value proposition: A stand-on body-fat analyzer marketed as a medical-grade health tool for tracking BMI and body composition, sold through retail channels with professional-grade accuracy.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the 10‑week, €15,000 survey test with 500 Japanese adults to compare purchase intent under health-necessity versus fitness-performance framing.. Uncertainty: Both T1 (health-necessity demand) and T2 (fitness-performance demand) remain uncertain due to lack of direct consumer purchase data from 1993 Japan.. Would change if: If the survey shows purchase intent ≥ 40% under health framing and ≤ 30% under fitness framing, T1 would be better supported and we would recommend a health-focused consumer proposition.; If the survey shows purchase intent ≥ 40% under fitness framing and ≤ 30% under health framing, T2 would be better supported and we would recommend a fitness-focused consumer proposition.; If both framing show ≥ 40% intent, the evidence would be inconclusive and we would recommend no expansion.. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

sources.excerpt: The Neumann Home Studio Academy offers high-quality tutorial videos on various aspects of recording via a dedicated website and an associated YouTube channel
The videos, which have met with an extremely positive response in recent years, are often described by viewers as being the best in this field.

As restrictions subsided and individuals returned to their normal lives, the pro audio equipment market for home studio content creation has been forced to re-stabilise from unsustainable pandemic levels. Global economic constraints have applied further pressure to revenues in 2022 and 2023 due to reduced consumer spending.
For us, this marks the perfect mic for the committed home studio owner who is looking to upgrade from whatever starter gear they had to proper pro-level equipment.
Meanwhile, Sennheiser will now devote its focus entirely to pro audio, business communications and the Neumann brand.

Unlike some other established microphone manufacturers, Neumann have resisted the urge to produce cheaper models by building them in the Far East, but their TLM range does at least contain some mics that fall into the category of 'affordable' — and these are clearly aimed at the wider project‑studio market as well as professional studio and broadcast applications.

events.text: Objective: Determine whether Neumann should create a differentiated proposition for home-studio creators and other individual buyers beyond its existing professional studio offering, or keep one professional range for everyone, based on evidence of market demand, current individual buyer reach, and potential value capture.. Constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.; Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.; Must consider at least three alternatives, including no expansion.; Evidence must be sourced from independent studies, market facts, or customer observations, not just company claims.. Alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated proposition for home-studio creators and individual buyers (new product line or marketing emphasis).; 2) Keep one professional range for everyone (no differentiation, same products for all segments).; 3) No expansion: maintain current product range and focus on professional studio market only.; 4) Expand into individual buyers via a different route (e.g., direct-to-consumer online store) without creating a differentiated proposition..

T1: Home-studio creators and individual buyers will adopt a differentiated Neumann proposition if it offers high-quality tutorials and community support, because they need expert guidance and peer validation to justify premium pricing. Who benefits: Neumann benefits by capturing higher margins from creators who value learning and community, and by building brand loyalty among creators who become advocates.. Why behaviour changes: Creators currently rely on generic online tutorials and forums; a dedicated academy with expert-led content creates a perceived value advantage over generic equipment, prompting them to choose Neumann over competitors.. How value is captured: Neumann can charge premium prices for microphones and accessories, and sell subscription services for exclusive tutorials, while creators pay for access to the academy, creating a dual revenue stream.. Assumptions: Creators are willing to pay for expert-led learning resources.; The Neumann brand is associated with high-quality audio and professional expertise.; Community features (forums, peer feedback) increase perceived value.. Predictions: Creators will report higher satisfaction with product and learning experience compared to generic alternatives.; Purchase intent for Neumann products will increase when presented with academy-branded content.; Subscription renewal rates for the academy will be higher among creators who have completed at least one course..

T2: Home-studio creators and individual buyers will adopt a differentiated Neumann proposition if it offers a subscription model that provides exclusive access to premium content (tutorials, masterclasses) and a community platform, because they seek ongoing learning and networking that justifies recurring payment. Who benefits: Neumann benefits by capturing recurring revenue from creators who value continuous learning and community, and by building a loyal creator ecosystem that can be monetized through additional services.. Why behaviour changes: Creators currently rely on free or generic online resources; a subscription model with curated content and community features creates a perceived value advantage over free alternatives, prompting them to choose Neumann's subscription over. How value is captured: Neumann can charge a monthly fee for access to exclusive tutorials, masterclasses, and community forums, while creators pay for ongoing learning and networking, creating a sustainable revenue stream.. Assumptions: Creators are willing to pay for exclusive, expert-led content.; Community features (forums, peer feedback) increase perceived value and engagement.; Recurring revenue is more predictable than one-time sales.. Predictions: Creators will report higher satisfaction with content and community compared to generic alternatives.; Subscription renewal rates will be higher among creators who have completed at least one course.; Purchase intent for Neumann products will increase when presented with subscription-branded content..

Test "Subscription vs Academy Proposition Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Two groups receive a product description of a Neumann microphone and a brief overview of the Neumann Home Studio Academy (existing tutorial videos). Group A is offered a subscription to the Academy with access to exclusive tutorials and community forum; Group B is offered a discounted price on the same microphone with no subscription. Both groups are asked to indicate willingness to pay (WTP) on a 7‑point scale and their preferred option. The test also collects demographic data (age, experience level, current gear).. Sample: 200 home‑studio creators and individual buyers, recruited via social media and creator forums, balanced between beginners and experienced users.. Measure: Average WTP for the subscription offer (Group A) and the discounted offer (Group B), and the percentage of participants choosing the subscription over the discount.. Predictions: T1: Group A’s average WTP will be at least 1.5 points higher than Group B’s average WTP, and the subscription choice rate will be at least 15 percentage points higher than the discount choice rate.; T2: Group A’s average WTP will not differ significantly from Group B’s average WTP, and the subscription choice rate will be at most 5 percentage points higher than the discount choice rate.. Decision rule: If Group A’s average WTP ≥ 1.5 points higher than Group B’s average WTP AND the subscription choice rate ≥ 15 percentage points higher than the discount choice rate – adopt the differentiated subscription proposition (supports T2). T1: Outdoor recreation enthusiasts will adopt 406 MHz distress beacons because they provide a reliable emergency backup in remote areas where other communication methods fail. Who benefits: Hikers, climbers, and other outdoor users who need a safety device that can be used in life-threatening situations.. Why behaviour changes: These users currently rely on mobile phones, radio, or satellite phones, but these can be damaged, lost, or out of range. A distress beacon offers a redundant, automatic alert that can be activated without user intervention.. How value is captured: ACR can sell the beacons directly to consumers through outdoor retailers or online, capturing the full retail price. The company also benefits from recurring revenue through rental or maintenance contracts.. Assumptions: Outdoor recreation participation rates in the U.S. remain stable or grow in 2002.; Consumers are willing to pay a premium for safety devices that work in remote environments.; Distribution channels (retailers, online) can reach this demographic.. Predictions: Surveyed outdoor recreation participants will indicate a willingness to purchase a 406 MHz distress beacon at a price point of $300-500.; Sales of the beacon will be concentrated in regions with high outdoor activity (e.g., national parks, mountain ranges)..

T2: Emergency preparedness organizations and government agencies will adopt 406 MHz distress beacons because they provide a standardized, interoperable solution for remote search and rescue, reducing response time and cost. Who benefits: Search and rescue (SAR) agencies, emergency management offices, and government departments responsible for public safety.. Why behaviour changes: Current SAR systems rely on multiple radio frequencies and protocols, leading to interoperability issues. A standardized 406 MHz distress beacon can be tracked by existing satellite networks, providing a single-source alert that can be used. How value is captured: ACR can sell the beacons to governments and NGOs at bulk rates, securing long-term contracts and recurring revenue from maintenance and upgrades. The company also benefits from brand association with reliable emergency. Assumptions: Government procurement cycles for emergency equipment are active in 2002.; Interoperability is a critical requirement for SAR agencies.; Price sensitivity is lower for public sector buyers compared to consumer markets.. Predictions: Government procurement requests for 406 MHz distress beacons will increase in 2002.; Sales will be concentrated in regions with high SAR demand (e.g., mountain ranges, remote coastal areas)..

Test "Fashion vs Safety Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with two variant versions of a product description for a new, stylish earplug designed for musicians. Version A emphasizes fashion and status (e.g., "Elevate your sound with style" and visible color options). Version B emphasizes safety and regulatory compliance (e.g., "Meet OSHA standards for hearing protection" and visible compliance certifications). Participants are randomly assigned to one version and asked to indicate purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and willingness to pay a premium (percentage above standard price).. Sample: 500 adults aged 18–45 who have attended live music events in the past year, recruited via an online panel.. Measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) and premium willingness (percentage above standard price).. Predictions: T1: Version A will yield a purchase intent score at least 15 percentage points higher than Version B and a premium willingness at least 20% higher.; T2: Version B will yield a purchase intent score at least 15 percentage points higher than Version A and a premium willingness at least 20% higher.. Decision rule: If Version A’s purchase intent ≥ 7.5 and premium willingness ≥ 20% → adopt fashion messaging. If Version B’s purchase intent ≥ 7.5 and premium willingness ≥ 20% → adopt safety messaging. If neither meets thresholds, both theories remain uncertain.. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not commit to a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Instead, conduct a low‑cost test (e.g., the proposed fashion vs safety messaging survey) to gather real purchase intent data before investing further. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Test "Fashion vs. Functional Purchase Intent Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Participants view two versions of a Hellberg earplug: a standard model and a styled version with visible branding, color, and design elements. They are asked to indicate purchase intent (1‑10) and willingness to pay a premium (percentage above standard price). The survey also captures self‑identified interest in fashion/style and activity‑specific use.. Sample: 500 adults aged 18–45, recruited via an online panel, balanced for gender and interest in fashion/activity‑related products.. Measure: Mean purchase intent score for each version; mean premium willingness for each version; correlation between fashion‑interest score and purchase intent for styled version; correlation between activity‑interest score and purchase intent for functional version.. Predictions: T1: Higher purchase intent and premium willingness for the styled version; strong positive correlation between fashion interest and purchase intent for styled version.; T2: Higher purchase intent and premium willingness for the functional version; strong positive correlation between activity interest and purchase intent for functional version.. Decision rule: If the mean purchase intent for the styled version exceeds the mean for the functional version by at least 1.5 points (on a 1‑10 scale) AND the premium willingness for the styled version exceeds the functional version by at least 10 percentage points, then T1 is supported. If the opposite pattern holds, T2 is supported. If neither. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Decision rule: If musicians’ choice rate ≥ 15% higher than industrial workers → adopt T1. If industrial workers’ choice rate ≥ 15% higher than musicians → adopt T2. T1: Home-studio creators and individual buyers will adopt a differentiated Neumann proposition if it offers high-quality tutorials and community support, because they need expert guidance and peer validation to justify premium pricing. Who benefits: Neumann benefits by capturing higher margins from creators who value learning and community, and by building brand loyalty among creators who become advocates.. Why behaviour changes: Creators currently rely on generic online tutorials and forums; a dedicated academy with expert-led content creates a perceived value advantage over generic equipment, prompting them to choose Neumann over competitors.. How value is captured: Neumann can charge premium prices for microphones and accessories, and sell subscription services for exclusive tutorials, while creators pay for access to the academy, creating a dual revenue stream.. Assumptions: Creators are willing to pay for expert-led learning resources.; The Neumann brand is associated with high-quality audio and professional expertise.; Community features (forums, peer feedback) increase perceived value.. Predictions: Creators will report higher satisfaction with product and learning experience compared to generic alternatives.; Purchase intent for Neumann products will increase when presented with academy-branded content.; Subscription renewal rates for the academy will be higher among creators who have completed at least one course..

T2: Home-studio creators and individual buyers will adopt a differentiated Neumann proposition if it offers a subscription model that provides exclusive access to premium content (tutorials, masterclasses) and a community platform, because they seek ongoing learning and networking that justifies recurring payment. Who benefits: Neumann benefits by capturing recurring revenue from creators who value continuous learning and community, and by building a loyal creator ecosystem that can be monetized through additional services.. Why behaviour changes: Creators currently rely on free or generic online resources; a subscription model with curated content and community features creates a perceived value advantage over free alternatives, prompting them to choose Neumann's subscription over. How value is captured: Neumann can charge a monthly fee for access to exclusive tutorials, masterclasses, and community forums, while creators pay for ongoing learning and networking, creating a sustainable revenue stream.. Assumptions: Creators are willing to pay for exclusive, expert-led content.; Community features (forums, peer feedback) increase perceived value and engagement.; Recurring revenue is more predictable than one-time sales.. Predictions: Creators will report higher satisfaction with content and community compared to generic alternatives.; Subscription renewal rates will be higher among creators who have completed at least one course.; Purchase intent for Neumann products will increase when presented with subscription-branded content..

Participants are recruited from a panel of home-studio creators and individual buyers. They are randomly assigned to one of two conditions: Condition A receives a link to a simulated subscription landing page offering exclusive tutorials and community access for a monthly fee; Condition B receives a link to a simulated academy landing page offering the same tutorials and community access via a one-time purchase. Participants are asked to indicate their intent to sign up (binary choice) and to. Sample: 200 participants: 100 creators (defined as those who report creating content for platforms like YouTube, Twitch, or social media) and 100 individual buyers (defined as those who purchase equipment for personal use). Recruit via creator forums, social media, and general consumer panels.. Measure: Primary outcome: purchase intent (binary: "Would sign up for subscription/academy"?). Secondary outcomes: willingness to pay (EUR amount) and perceived value (1‑10 scale).. Predictions: T1: Creators in Condition A will report higher purchase intent than creators in Condition B, because the subscription model aligns with their need for expert-led learning.; T2: All participants regardless of creator status will report higher purchase intent in Condition A than Condition B, because the subscription model offers ongoing exclusive content and community.. Decision rule: If creators in Condition A have purchase intent ≥60% and creators in Condition B have intent <40%, proceed with differentiated subscription proposition (supports T2). If creators in Condition B have purchase intent ≥60% and creators in Condition A have intent <40%, proceed with differentiated academy proposition (supports T1). If both conditions meet the 60% threshold, both. Cost: 15000 euros, 8 weeks.

sources.excerpt: An interesting side note is that in 1959, according to Lee Wannie, who was an engineering department draftsman at John Deere’s Horicon plant, a prototype lawn and garden tractor had been built at their factory.
Deere had purchased several competitive lawn and garden tractors to make evaluations on pros and cons of each brand.

Using a hydrostatic drive for the variable ground speed had advantages but was cost prohibitive to be competitive in the marketplace.
Production of the company’s first lawn and garden tractor began at Horicon in 1963, when John Deere built 1000 units of the 110 model.
The company ventures into the consumer market, deciding to produce and sell lawn and garden tractors plus some attachments such as mowers and snow blowers.
The demand for garden tractors was rapidly increasing as households with small gardens found them rather inexpensive, practical to use for a variety of chores, and they were economical to maintain.

Who benefits: Homeowners gain a versatile garden tool; Deere gains sales volume through a new consumer segment.. Why behaviour changes: Rapidly increasing demand for garden tractors indicates that cost-effectiveness and multi-use capability drive purchase decisions.. How value is captured: Deere can sell tractors directly to consumers at a modest price point, leveraging its existing manufacturing capacity and dealer network to reach buyers without major retooling.. T2: Homeowners will adopt lawn tractors because they represent a status symbol and a symbol of modern home ownership, leading to purchase driven by prestige and desire for a modern garden tool. Who benefits: Homeowners gain a status item that signals modern living; Deere gains premium pricing and brand association beyond functional utility.. Why behaviour changes: As home ownership becomes more widespread and gardens become part of suburban lifestyle, buyers seek tools that signal modern lifestyle and social status.. How value is captured: Deere can price tractors at a premium, sell through existing dealer network, and market them as a lifestyle product rather than just a garden tool.. Assumptions: Homeowners associate garden tools with personal identity and social status.; Modern branding and design are valued by buyers beyond functional need.; Deere can design a tractor that looks distinctive and appeals to lifestyle aspirations.. Test "Price vs Prestige Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Randomized controlled online survey with two parallel groups. Group A sees a low-price, functional description of a lawn tractor (cost-effectiveness message). Group B sees a high-price, design-focused description emphasizing status and modern lifestyle (prestige message). Both groups are asked about purchase intent on a 1‑10 scale and willingness to pay a fixed price. The test also collects demographic data (age, household income, home ownership status).. Sample: 200 U.S. homeowners recruited via an online panel, balanced across age and income brackets. 100 per group.. Measure: Average purchase intent score (1‑10) and average willingness to pay (EUR).. Predictions: T1: Group A’s average purchase intent and willingness to pay will be higher than Group B’s, because cost-effectiveness drives demand.; T2: Group B’s average purchase intent and willingness to pay will be higher than Group A’s, because status and prestige motivate buyers.. Decision rule: If Group A’s average willingness to pay exceeds Group B’s by at least €100 and its purchase intent is at least 1.5 points higher on the 1‑10 scale, then T1 is supported. If Group B’s willingness to pay exceeds Group A’s by at least €100 and its purchase intent is at least 1.5 points higher, then T2 is supported. If neither condition is met, both theories remain uncertain.. Cost: 15000 euros, 6 weeks.

Favours T1: Conduct the proposed Price vs Prestige Messaging Test to empirically compare cost-effectiveness messaging against prestige messaging. The test will determine whether price-driven demand (T1) or prestige-driven demand (T2) is more likely in 1962. Until results are available, both theories remain uncertain and any investment decision should be delayed. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Conduct the proposed Price vs Prestige Messaging Test to empirically compare cost-effectiveness messaging against prestige messaging. The test will determine whether price-driven demand (T1) or prestige-driven demand (T2) is more likely in 1962. Next action: Run the 6‑week, €15,000 online survey test with 200 U.S. homeowners, measuring purchase intent and willingness to pay under cost‑effectiveness versus prestige messaging.. Uncertainty: Both theories remain uncertain due to lack of direct evidence on buyer motivations in 1962.. Would change if: If the test shows Group A’s willingness to pay exceeds Group B’s by at least €100 and its purchase intent is at least 1.5 points higher, T1 would be supported and the recommendation would shift to develop a low‑priced consumer line.; If Group B’s willingness to pay exceeds Group A’s by at least €100 and its purchase intent is at least 1.5 points higher, T2 would be supported and the recommendation would shift to develop a prestige‑branded line.; If neither condition is met, both theories remain uncertain and the recommendation would remain to test before committing.. Based on medical evidence linking excess body fat to heart disease, diabetes and certain cancers, Tanita introduced the world’s first integrated body composition analyzer/scale to the professional markets in 1992.
Tanita is a world leader in precision electronic scales. With almost 50% of its domestic market share, the name Tanita is a household name in Japan.
In Japan, every household has a bathroom scale (health meter), and most nowadays keep track of your body composition.
In 104 men and 101 women (16-78 years and BMI 16-41 kg/m2) the mean bias in body-fat mass measured using the Tanita body-fat analyser was 0.8 (2SD 7.9) kg relative to a four-compartment model.
These findings indicate the need for controlled measurement conditions to obtain valid body composition estimates using the TBI method in healthy people.
The Tanita TBF-310 foot-to-foot BIA body composition analyser with the manufacturer's prediction equations is not recommended for application to individual children who are overweight and obese
The prevalence of preobese (BMI: 25-29.9kg m(-2)) and obese (BMI > or = 30 kg m(-2)) men increased from 14.5% and 0.8%, respectively, in the time-period 1976-80 to 20.5% and 2.01% during 1991-95.

An interesting side note is that in 1959, according to Lee Wannie, who was an engineering department draftsman at John Deere’s Horicon plant, a prototype lawn and garden tractor had been built at their factory.
Deere had purchased several competitive lawn and garden tractors to make evaluations on pros and cons of each brand.
Because of this, many John Deere dealers were selling some of these lines or other brands of lawn and garden tractors because Deere didn’t offer any.
Production of the company’s first lawn and garden tractor began at Horicon in 1963, when John Deere built 1000 units of the 110 model.
The company ventures into the consumer market, deciding to produce and sell lawn and garden tractors plus some attachments such as mowers and snow blowers.
The demand for garden tractors was rapidly increasing as households with small gardens found them rather inexpensive, practical to use for a variety of chores, and they were economical to maintain.
In 1869, Charles began to introduce marketing centers and independent retail dealers to advance the company's sales nationwide.

Constraints: Limited to public sources published before mid-1962; no internal company data.; Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.; Evidence must address demand, willingness to pay, and feasibility of reaching individual buyers.; Must consider existing dealer network and any existing consumer products.. T1: Homeowners will adopt lawn tractors because they view them as a time‑saving, convenient way to maintain their yards, and they are willing to pay a premium for a reliable brand. Who benefits: Homeowners seeking efficient yard care; Deere benefits by capturing higher margins through premium pricing and brand loyalty.. Why behaviour changes: Growing suburban population and increasing disposable income make yard care a desirable home improvement; a tractor offers faster, easier mowing than hand tools.. How value is captured: Deere can charge a higher price for its brand and service, and sell accessories and maintenance contracts, creating recurring revenue.. Assumptions: Suburban growth in the 1960s will increase demand for lawn care tools.; Homeowners associate brand reputation with quality and are willing to pay more.; Deere can produce a reliable, easy‑to‑use tractor that meets homeowner needs.. Predictions: Surveyed homeowners will indicate willingness to pay at least 1.5 times the price of a generic lawn mower for a tractor.; Sales of tractors will correlate with growth in suburban housing starts..

T2: Homeowners will adopt lawn tractors because they view them as a status symbol and a way to demonstrate modern living, and they are willing to pay a premium for a brand that signals wealth and sophistication. Who benefits: Homeowners seeking to show social status and modern lifestyle; Deere benefits by capturing premium pricing and brand equity.. Why behaviour changes: Post-WWII suburban growth creates a culture where yard care is a visible display of affluence; a tractor is seen as a symbol of modern home ownership.. How value is captured: Deere can charge higher prices and sell through premium retail channels, leveraging brand prestige to justify premium margins.. Assumptions: Suburban homeowners associate lawn care with social status.; Brand reputation is a primary purchase driver for lawn tractors.; Deere can position its tractors as a status item through marketing and design.. Predictions: Surveyed homeowners will rank brand prestige as a top purchase criterion for a lawn tractor.; Sales will be higher in affluent suburban neighborhoods than in urban areas..

Test "Homeowner Survey Test: Time‑Saving vs Status Messaging" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Participants view a product description of a 1962‑era lawn tractor (specifications, price, and a brief description emphasizing either time‑saving/convenience or status/modern lifestyle). They are asked: "How much would you be willing to pay for this tractor?" (open‑ended). They also rate the tractor on a 1‑10 scale for perceived time‑saving (1‑. Sample: 500 homeowners recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and region (suburban vs urban).. Measure: Average willingness‑to‑pay (EUR) for the time‑saving description versus the status description.. Predictions: T1: Average willingness‑to‑pay will be higher for the time‑saving description than for the status description.; T2: Average willingness‑to‑pay will be higher for the status description than for the time‑saving description.. Decision rule: If the average willingness‑to‑pay for the time‑saving description exceeds the average for the status description by at least €150 (a 20% premium), we conclude T1 is better supported. If the status description exceeds the time‑saving description by at least €150, we conclude T2 is better supported. If the difference is less than €150, both theories remain uncertain.. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Conduct the proposed homeowner survey test (X1) to compare willingness to pay for time‑saving versus status messaging. If the test shows a €150 premium for the time‑saving description, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting time‑saving homeowners; otherwise, maintain focus on existing B2B markets and dealer network. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Value proposition: A differentiated lawn tractor offering superior time‑saving performance, built‑in accessories, and a premium brand promise, sold through existing dealer network with training to highlight convenience benefits.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the 10‑week, €15,000 homeowner survey test (X1) to measure willingness to pay for time‑saving versus status messaging.. Uncertainty: The evidence base is limited to a single independent source (deere-wheelhorse-demand) that supports T1. Would change if: If the test shows a €150 premium for the status description, we would shift focus to a status‑driven proposition.; If the test shows no significant premium for either description, we would recommend no expansion and maintain the existing dealer model.. sources.excerpt: Based on medical evidence linking excess body fat to heart disease, diabetes and certain cancers, Tanita introduced the world’s first integrated body composition analyzer/scale to the professional markets in 1992.
Tanita is a world leader in precision electronic scales. With almost 50% of its domestic market share, the name Tanita is a household name in Japan.
In Japan, every household has a bathroom scale (health meter), and most nowadays keep track of your body composition.
In 104 men and 101 women (16-78 years and BMI 16-41 kg/m2) the mean bias in body-fat mass measured using the Tanita body-fat analyser was 0.8 (2SD 7.9) kg relative to a four-compartment model.
These findings indicate the need for controlled measurement conditions to obtain valid body composition estimates using the TBI method in healthy people.
The Tanita TBF-310 foot-to-foot BIA body composition analyser with the manufacturer's prediction equations is not recommended for application to individual children who are overweight and obese
The prevalence of preobese (BMI: 25-29.9kg m(-2)) and obese (BMI > or = 30 kg m(-2)) men increased from 14.5% and 0.8%, respectively, in the time-period 1976-80 to 20.5% and 2.01% during 1991-95.

T1: Health‑conscious households will adopt a stand‑on body‑fat analyser as a home health tool because they value precise body composition data for personal fitness and disease prevention. Who benefits: Health‑conscious individuals and their families who currently monitor weight and body composition using bathroom scales or other methods.. Why behaviour changes: Public health messaging in Japan (and other developed markets) links excess body fat to conditions like heart disease and diabetes, creating demand for accurate, actionable body composition data.. How value is captured: Tanita can capture value by selling the device as a premium health monitor directly to consumers, leveraging its existing brand trust in household weighing devices and the accuracy demonstrated in clinical trials.. Assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a premium for body composition measurement over basic weighing.; Tanita’s existing household scale reputation transfers to new product acceptance.; Regulatory environment allows home use of medical‑grade body‑fat analyzers in 1993.. Predictions: A survey of 500 Japanese households would show >30% intent to purchase a stand‑on body‑fat analyser at a price of ¥15,000 (approx. $130 USD).; Sales would be driven by purchases motivated by health concerns rather than price sensitivity..

T2: Fitness enthusiasts and athletes will adopt a stand‑on body‑fat analyser because they need precise, real‑time data for training and performance tracking, and they are willing to invest in advanced equipment. Who benefits: Fitness clubs, personal trainers, and individual athletes who currently rely on subjective assessments or basic scales for body composition monitoring.. Why behaviour changes: Growing popularity of fitness and weight‑training culture in Japan and other developed markets creates a demand for data‑driven performance measurement that is not satisfied by existing tools.. How value is captured: Tanita can capture value by positioning the device as a professional‑grade tool for clubs and trainers, and by offering subscription services for data analysis and training plans, leveraging its clinical‑grade accuracy.. Assumptions: Fitness market in Japan is large enough to support premium pricing for body‑fat analyzers.; Athletes value precise data for training adjustments.; Regulatory environment permits home‑use devices for professional‑grade applications in 1993.. Predictions: A survey of 300 fitness club members would show >25% intent to purchase the device at a price of ¥20,000 (approx. $170 USD) for professional use.; Purchase decisions would be driven by performance‑related benefits rather than health concerns..

Predictions: T1: Condition A (fashion version) will have a higher average purchase intent and willingness-to-pay than Condition B.; T2: Condition B (communication version) will have a higher average purchase intent and willingness-to-pay than Condition A.. Who benefits: Small‑holder farmers and homeowners with small gardens who need a machine that can perform multiple chores (e.g., till, mow, pull small equipment).. Why behaviour changes: These users currently rely on manual tools or cheaper garden tractors; a Deere tractor offers improved efficiency, reliability, and the convenience of a single machine for various tasks. How value is captured: Deere sells tractors at a price premium reflecting its engineering and brand reputation, and earns recurring revenue through dealer‑sold accessories, maintenance, and parts.. Who benefits: Neumann benefits by capturing higher margins from creators who value learning and community, and by building brand loyalty among creators who become advocates.. Why behaviour changes: Creators currently rely on generic online tutorials and forums; a dedicated academy with expert-led content creates a perceived value advantage over generic equipment, prompting them to choose Neumann over competitors.. How value is captured: Neumann can charge premium prices for microphones and accessories, and sell subscription services for exclusive tutorials, while creators pay for access to the academy, creating a dual revenue stream.. Predictions: Creators will report higher satisfaction with product and learning experience compared to generic alternatives.; Purchase intent for Neumann products will increase when presented with academy-branded content.; Subscription renewal rates for the academy will be higher among creators who have completed at least one course..

T2: Home-studio creators and individual buyers will adopt a differentiated Neumann proposition if it offers a subscription model that provides exclusive access to premium content (tutorials, masterclasses) and a community platform, because they seek ongoing learning and networking that justifies recurring payment. Who benefits: Neumann benefits by capturing recurring revenue from creators who value continuous learning and community, and by building a loyal creator ecosystem that can be monetized through additional services.. Why behaviour changes: Creators currently rely on free or generic online resources; a subscription model with curated content and community features creates a perceived value advantage over free alternatives, prompting them to choose Neumann's subscription over. How value is captured: Neumann can charge a monthly fee for access to exclusive tutorials, masterclasses, and community forums, while creators pay for ongoing learning and networking, creating a sustainable revenue stream.. Assumptions: Creators are willing to pay for exclusive, expert-led content.; Community features (forums, peer feedback) increase perceived value and engagement.; Recurring revenue is more predictable than one-time sales.. Predictions: Creators will report higher satisfaction with content and community compared to generic alternatives.; Subscription renewal rates will be higher among creators who have completed at least one course.; Purchase intent for Neumann products will increase when presented with subscription-branded content..

Test "Subscription vs Tutorial-Only Proposition Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey experiment with two arms. Participants are recruited from a panel of home-studio creators and individual buyers who have shown interest in Neumann products. They are randomly assigned to one of two groups. Group A sees a presentation of a differentiated proposition that includes a subscription model offering exclusive tutorials, masterclasses, and community access (as per T2). Group B sees a presentation of a differentiated proposition that includes only high-quality. Sample: 300 participants: 150 from Group A (subscription model) and 150 from Group B (tutorial-only model). Recruit via a panel that captures creators from both entry-level and professional segments.. Measure: Purchase intent: binary (would buy a Neumann microphone within 3 months). Secondary: willingness to pay for subscription (EUR amount).. Predictions: T1: Group B (tutorial-only) will have higher purchase intent than Group A (subscription) because creators value expert-led learning and are willing to pay for it.; T2: Group A (subscription) will have higher purchase intent than Group B (tutorial-only) because creators seek ongoing learning and networking that justifies recurring payment.. Decision rule: If Group A purchase intent >= 35% and Group B purchase intent <= 20%, then the evidence supports T2 (subscription model). If Group B purchase intent >= 35% and Group A purchase intent <= 20%, then the evidence supports T1 (tutorial-only).. Cost: 18000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not commit to a differentiated proposition yet. Instead, run a low-cost survey experiment (as proposed in test X1) to test whether creators prefer a subscription model with exclusive content or a tutorial-only proposition. The €18,000 budget and 10‑week timeline are sufficient to gather valid results. Until we have evidence, keep the current professional range and focus on the existing Neumann brand for all segmen Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.
